module_title: Plant Physiology Basics: Photosynthesis, Respiration & Growth (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: Plant physiology is the study of the vital processes occurring in plants. This foundational level introduces the two most critical biochemical pathways in the biosphere: Photosynthesis (building energy) and Cellular Respiration (releasing energy), along with the chemical messengers (Plant Growth Regulators) that dictate plant development.

core_concepts.title: Photosynthesis: Site and Pigments
core_concepts.description:
Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process by which plants use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds. 
- Site: Occurs in the Chloroplasts. The membranous system (Grana and Stroma lamellae) is responsible for trapping light energy and synthesizing ATP and NADPH (Light Reactions). The Stroma (fluid matrix) contains enzymes for the enzymatic reduction of $CO_2$ into carbohydrates (Dark Reactions).
- Pigments: Chlorophyll a (the chief/primary photosynthetic pigment, blue-green), Chlorophyll b (yellow-green), Xanthophylls (yellow), and Carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange). The accessory pigments (b, xanthophylls, carotenoids) absorb broader wavelengths of light and transfer the energy to Chlorophyll a, while also protecting Chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

core_concepts.title: Respiration in Plants: The Basics
core_concepts.description:
Cellular respiration is the breaking of C-C bonds of complex compounds through oxidation within the cells, releasing a considerable amount of energy trapped as ATP.
- Plants do not have specialized respiratory organs like lungs, but they possess stomata and lenticels for gaseous exchange.
- Aerobic Respiration: Complete oxidation of organic substances in the presence of oxygen, releasing $CO_2$, water, and a large amount of energy. Occurs in the Mitochondria.
- Anaerobic Respiration (Fermentation): Incomplete oxidation in the absence of oxygen. In plants/yeast, the end products are Ethanol and $CO_2$. Only yields 2 net ATP per glucose molecule.

core_concepts.title: Plant Growth and Development
core_concepts.description:
Growth in plants is largely restricted to specialized regions of active cell division called meristems (apical, lateral, intercalary). 
Phases of Growth:
1. Meristematic Phase: Cells at root/shoot apex. Rich in protoplasm, large nuclei, primary thin cellulosic cell walls with abundant plasmodesmata.
2. Elongation Phase: Proximal to the meristematic zone. Characterized by increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition.
3. Maturation Phase: Proximal to the elongation zone. Cells attain their maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications.

core_concepts.title: Plant Growth Regulators (PGRs) / Phytohormones
core_concepts.description:
PGRs are small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition. They are broadly divided into two groups:
1. Plant Growth Promoters: Involved in growth promoting activities like cell division, cell enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting, and seed formation. Examples: Auxins, Gibberellins (GAs), and Cytokinins.
2. Plant Growth Inhibitors: Involved in responses to wounds and stresses of biotic and abiotic origin. They promote dormancy and abscission. Examples: Abscisic Acid (ABA) and Ethylene. (Note: Ethylene largely acts as an inhibitor but has some promoter activities like fruit ripening).

important_entities.name: Action Spectrum vs. Absorption Spectrum
important_entities.key_fact: Chlorophyll 'a' shows maximum absorption and maximum photosynthetic action in the Blue and Red regions of the visible spectrum.
important_entities.significance: T.W. Engelmann demonstrated this using a prism to split light illuminating a green alga (Cladophora) placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria. The bacteria accumulated mainly in the blue and red light regions, providing the first functional action spectrum of photosynthesis.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A massive conceptual trap. The 'Dark Reaction' (Calvin Cycle) DOES NOT mean it only occurs in the dark or happens at night. It is merely called 'dark' because it is not *directly* light-driven. However, it is strictly dependent on the products of the light reaction (ATP and NADPH). If light becomes unavailable, the dark reaction will continue for a very short time until ATP/NADPH are exhausted, and then it stops entirely.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
NEET heavily tests the chemical derivatives of hormones:
- Auxins: Indole compounds (Indole-3-acetic acid / IAA).
- Cytokinins: Adenine derivatives ($N^6$-furfurylamino purine / Kinetin).
- Gibberellins: Terpenes.
- Abscisic acid (ABA): Derivatives of carotenoids.
- Ethylene: The only gaseous hormone ($C_2H_4$).

exam_strategy_tips: Always remember that Glycolysis is common to BOTH aerobic and anaerobic respiration. It occurs entirely in the cytoplasm and requires strictly ZERO oxygen. It is the only process of respiration in anaerobic organisms.
